warmup.q: A DynamoDB payments table has partition key accountId and sort key createdAt. You want merchant M-0042's payments from today. What does DynamoDB do with merchantId = 'M-0042'?
options: Uses the index DynamoDB builds automatically on every attribute
Can't run it as a Query: you either Scan the whole table or add an index keyed by merchant
Hashes M-0042 to find the right partition, like any other key
Reads only today's items, because createdAt is the sort key
warmup.why: A DynamoDB Query must give the partition key with =, and merchantId isn't part of this table's key. The store has no automatic indexes, and hashing a merchant id tells it nothing about where accounts live. Without a global secondary index on the merchant, the only way is a Scan that reads every item and filters.

sections.h: A distributed store finds data only by its key
sections.html:
Lesson 1 ended on a rule: in the models beyond tables, the key decides which questions are cheap. This lesson turns that rule into a method. Start with what you're used to. In Oracle you can filter on any column. WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' runs even without an index: the database reads the whole table from its own disks, and if that's too slow you add an index and the optimizer starts using it. One machine holds everything, so there is always a way.

Now spread 50 million payments over 40 partitions on 40 machines. A partition, from lesson 1 of this track, is one slice of the data held by one machine or one small group of machines. A query that doesn't say which partition holds its answer has to ask all 40, and each one has to read everything it holds. DynamoDB and Cassandra refuse to work that way by default. They find data by key and only by key, so you design the key around the questions. Build one up for a single question: "account A-1001's 20 newest payments".

Version 1 keys each payment by its payment id. The store hashes the id to choose a partition, the way Dynamo did in lesson 1. Fetching one payment by id touches one partition and one item. But A-1001's payments are scattered over all 40 partitions, so the question has to visit all 40.

Version 2 keys each payment by its account id. All of A-1001's payments now share a key, so they land in the same partition. This part of the key is the partition key. The store hashes it, so it can only answer "equals this value", and only when you give all of it. A busy account has 30,000 payments, though, and inside the partition nothing says which are the newest. The store would read all 30,000 and sort them to return 20.

Version 3 adds a second part to the key, the sort key, here the creation time. Inside a partition the store keeps items sorted by it, as Bigtable keeps rows sorted. "The 20 newest" becomes: go to A-1001's partition, start at the end, step back 20 items. Every item now has an address in two parts: the partition key says which partition, the sort key says where inside it. That's the picture for this lesson. Every design below is a choice of address.

The address gives every query one of three outcomes:

  • A key lookup gives the whole address with =. On the table, that's one item.
  • A range read gives the partition key with = and a range or an order on the sort key. It reads one run of neighbouring items, and its cost grows with what it returns.
  • A scan is everything else. The store reads items and throws some away, at best one whole partition, at worst the whole table.

The demo below puts 200,000 payments in one sorted map and counts what each kind of question touches.

try.title: Count what each question touches
steps: Read AccessPathDemo.kt. It loads 200,000 payments into one TreeMap, keyed accountId#createdAt#paymentId, the way a store keeps items sorted inside its partitions. The merchant is only in the value.
Predict how many entries each question touches: one payment by its full key, account A-00042's newest 20, and all of merchant M-0042's payments.

code.title: AccessPathDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l02.demo import java.util.TreeMap /** The key of payment number i: accountId # createdAt # paymentId. */ private fun keyOf(i: Int): String { val account = "A-%05d".format(i % 10_000) val createdAt = "2026-11-%02dT%02d:%02d".format(1 + i % 7, (i / 7) % 24, (i / 168) % 60) return "$account#$createdAt#pay-$i" } /** 200,000 payments in one sorted map, keyed account#time#payment. Three questions, three costs. */ fun main() { // the value is the merchant, which is NOT part of the key val payments = TreeMap<String, String>() for (i in 0 until 200_000) payments[keyOf(i)] = "M-%04d".format(i % 997) fun timed(label: String, block: () -> Pair<Int, Int>) { var result = 0 to 0 val nanos = (1..21).map { // run it 21 times, report the median val t0 = System.nanoTime() result = block() System.nanoTime() - t0 }.sorted()[10] println("%-34s found %4d, touched %,7d entries, about %,9d ns".format(label, result.first, result.second, nanos)) } // 1. the full key: one lookup val oneKey = keyOf(160_042) timed("key lookup (full key)") { (if (payments[oneKey] != null) 1 else 0) to 1 } // 2. the account is the key's prefix: one contiguous slice, read from the end for newest first timed("A-00042's newest 20 (range read)") { val slice = payments.subMap("A-00042#", true, "A-00042$", false).descendingMap() // '$' comes right after '#' val newest = slice.entries.take(20) newest.size to newest.size } // 3. the merchant is not in the key: nothing to jump to, so look at everything timed("merchant M-0042's payments (scan)") { var touched = 0 var found = 0 for ((_, merchant) in payments) { touched++ if (merchant == "M-0042") found++ } found to touched } }

try.expect:
key lookup (full key)              found    1, touched       1 entries, about       625 ns
A-00042's newest 20 (range read)   found   20, touched      20 entries, about    14,208 ns
merchant M-0042's payments (scan)  found  201, touched 200,000 entries, about 3,683,584 ns

The entry counts are exact. The times are one run on an M-series laptop and move with your CPU and JIT warm-up. The merchant question has only 201 answers, but the map has to touch all 200,000 entries to find them, a few hundred times slower than the range read. Load a million payments and the range read still touches 20; the scan touches a million.

sections.h: Write the questions down before you choose the keys
sections.html:
The key from the last section answers one question well. A payments service asks several, and one key can't answer them all. So the first design artifact is a list of the questions, each written as the query your code will send. The Cassandra docs say it plainly: data modeling is query-driven. This list is called the access patterns. Here is the one every lab in this track uses:

# Access pattern As a query Rate
AP1 An account's payments, newest first account = ?, order by time high
AP2 A payment by id payment id = ? high
AP3 A merchant's payments with one status in a time window merchant = ?, status = ?, time between ? and ? medium
AP4 Has this idempotency key been used? idempotency key = ? every create
AP5 A transfer between two accounts, with ledger entries two accounts, all or nothing medium
AP6 The refunds of a payment payment id = ? low

Write each one with = for the values the code knows exactly and a range or an order for the rest. Put a rate next to each: it tells you where a scan is fine (a nightly export) and where it isn't (the authorization path, thousands of calls a second).

Then hold every pattern to one rule: it must be a key lookup or a range read. Check the first three against the address from the last section, partition key accountId and sort key createdAt. AP1 is a range read. AP2 gives a payment id, which isn't part of the address, so it's a scan. So is AP3.

When the address can't answer a pattern, you add a second copy of the data under a different address. In DynamoDB that copy is a global secondary index, which DynamoDB keeps up to date for you. In Cassandra it's another table that your code writes. In MongoDB it's another index. Every copy costs one more write on every insert. The stepper below walks AP1 to AP3 through this design, one copy at a time.

Two rules decide whether a copy's sort key can serve a pattern, and both follow from the sorted run.

No gaps: the sort key is used from left to right. With sort key (status, createdAt) the items are sorted by status first, then time. "FAILED since 09:00" is one run. "Any status since 09:00" is scattered across every status's run, so it isn't one read.

Filters cost what they read: a condition on an attribute outside the address, such as DynamoDB's FilterExpression, runs after the read. You pay for every item read, not every item returned.

This rigidity has a price. A new question next quarter can mean a new index, or rewriting old items to fill in a new key. Alex DeBrie, who argues for single-table design in DynamoDB, lists that inflexibility among its costs. You pay it in exchange for reads that stay fast at any size.

stepper.title: Three access patterns against one key design
stepper.intro: A payments table keyed by account and time. Watch which questions it answers, and what the fixes cost.

try.title: Predict the verdicts before the lab does
steps: Take the final design from the stepper: the table (accountId; createdAt), an index (merchantId; status, createdAt) and an index (paymentId).

For each query, write down key lookup, range read or scan, and which table or index serves it: (a) accountId = A-1001 AND createdAt BETWEEN 08:00 AND 12:00; (b) merchantId = M-0042 AND createdAt > 09:00; (c) merchantId = M-0042 AND status = FAILED, newest first; (d) accountId = A-1001 AND currency = EUR; (e) paymentId = pay-81741; (f) status = FAILED.
try.expect: (a) Range read on the table. (b) Scan: it skips status, so it reads all of M-0042's partition and filters by time. (c) Range read on the merchant index, read backward. (d) Scan: currency is outside every key, so it reads all of A-1001's items and filters. (e) Key lookup on the paymentId index. (f) Scan of everything: status is never a partition key. Notice that (b) and (d) read one partition, not the table. That's cheaper than (f), but the cost still grows with the partition instead of with the answer, which is why the lab's checker calls it a scan too.

video.title: Write the questions down, then choose the keys

sections.html:
Cassandra uses the same two-part address and goes one step further: its query language refuses a query that doesn't follow it. That language is CQL (Cassandra Query Language). It looks like SQL, but a table's primary key is the address, written in two parts:

CREATE TABLE payments_by_account (
    account_id   text,
    created_at   timestamp,
    payment_id   text,
    merchant_id  text,
    status       text,
    amount_minor bigint,
    currency     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, payment_id ASC);

The inner parentheses hold the partition key, account_id. Cassandra hashes it onto its ring of nodes, Dynamo style. The columns after it are clustering columns, Cassandra's name for the parts of the sort key: created_at, stored newest first, then payment_id, so two payments in the same millisecond don't overwrite each other. AP1 is now one partition read, already in the order the screen wants.

AP3 gets its own table, with an address built for the merchant:

PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id, day), status, created_at, payment_id)

The partition key has two parts. Without day, a busy merchant taking 40,000 payments a day would grow one partition without end, and the Cassandra docs advise keeping a partition under 100,000 values and 100 MB. Bucketing by day has its own price: a week of history is seven partition reads.

The service writes every payment to both tables. That's normal here: Cassandra's modeling guide says it duplicates data, and leans on cheap writes, to make reads fast. Lesson 5 shows why a Cassandra write is cheap: it's an append to a log plus an insert into a memtable, the LSM design from lesson 1. It also sizes the day bucket properly.

Ask a table a question its address can't answer, and CQL stops you with an error that names the escape hatch, ALLOW FILTERING. Add those words and the query runs by reading partitions and filtering them, with performance the docs call unpredictable. Treat that error as a design review: a table is missing.

try.title: Make CQL refuse a query
steps: From the labs folder, start Cassandra 5.0: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait. It takes about a minute to report healthy.
Load the two tables and six payments: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-02-payments.cql (no output means it worked).
Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh -k payments. Run the four queries below one at a time, and predict before each one whether it runs.
Stop Cassandra when you're done: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml down -v.

AP1: one partition, already stored newest first SELECT created_at, payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments_by_account WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' LIMIT 3; -- 2. the merchant is not in this table's key SELECT payment_id FROM payments_by_account WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042'; -- 3. AP3, on the table built for it SELECT status, created_at, payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments_by_merchant_day WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND day = '2026-11-07' AND status = 'FAILED' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000'; -- 4. the same, but skip the status clustering column SELECT payment_id FROM payments_by_merchant_day WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND day = '2026-11-07' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000';

Queries 1 and 3 run; 2 and 4 are refused (output trimmed):

sections.h: MongoDB: decide what lives in one document
sections.html:
MongoDB lets you index any field, so you never have to fit every question into one address. The question it hands you instead is about shape: what goes inside one document, and what stands on its own.

A document is a JSON-like record with nested objects and arrays; MongoDB stores it in a binary form called BSON, and a set of documents is a collection. Here is the choice for payments, as two collections:

// accounts: what the account screen shows, in one read
{ _id: "A-1001", customerId: "C-77", currency: "EUR",
  recentPayments: [ { id: "pay-81730", amountMinor: 4250 } /* the last 3 only */ ] }

// payments: one document each, pointing at its account
{ _id: "pay-81730", accountId: "A-1001", merchantId: "M-0043", status: "SETTLED",
  amountMinor: 4250, createdAt: ISODate("2026-11-07T10:30:12Z") }

Putting the recent payments inside the account is called embedding. Storing payments as their own documents that hold the account's id is called referencing. MongoDB's own guidance gives the rule. Embed what is read together, updated together, or belongs to its parent the way a line belongs to an invoice: one read returns it all, and a write to one document is atomic. Reference what has many entries, grows without bound, is written at different times from the parent, or makes sense by itself.

Payments grow without bound: an account keeps receiving them for years. Embed them all and the account document grows toward MongoDB's 16 MB document limit, and every read of the account drags the whole history along. A short, capped summary gives the screen what it needs in one read. $push with $slice adds to the array and trims it to a fixed length in one update.

The two-part address comes back in the indexes. A compound index is a sorted list of entries made from several fields, each entry pointing at its document, so it behaves like a sort key. MongoDB's ESR guideline orders the fields the same way as the no-gaps rule: equality fields first, then the sort field, then range fields. For AP3, { merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 } lets one walk of the index return a merchant's FAILED payments, newest first. Leave status out of the query and MongoDB can still use the index to find the merchant, but it has to sort the results in memory. It's the same rule as in Cassandra, enforced by cost instead of by an error.

try.title: Watch an index follow the access pattern
steps: From the labs folder, start MongoDB 9.0: docker compose -f env/mongo.yml up -d --wait (a few seconds).

Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/mongo.yml exec mongo mongosh sfz, then load the data: load("/sfz/nosql-02-payments.js"). It writes 1,000 payments for 50 accounts and defines cost(), which runs explain and keeps four numbers.
Run the blocks below in order. Before each cost(...), predict how many documents MongoDB examines to return 5.
Stop MongoDB when you're done: docker compose -f env/mongo.yml down -v.

code.title: in mongosh
code.html: // embed a bounded summary: the account keeps only its last 3 payments for (const p of db.payments.find({ accountId: "A-1001" }).sort({ createdAt: 1 }).limit(5)) { db.accounts.updateOne({ _id: "A-1001" }, { $push: { recentPayments: { $each: [{ id: p._id, amountMinor: p.amountMinor }], $slice: -3 } } }) } db.accounts.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }) // AP3 without an index, then with one in equality, sort, range order cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042", status: "FAILED" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5)) db.payments.createIndex({ merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }) cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042", status: "FAILED" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5)) // leave status out: the index finds the merchant, but the sort is no longer free cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5))

try.expect:
Output trimmed to the four results that matter, and folded onto fewer lines:

{ _id: 'A-1001', customerId: 'C-77', currency: 'EUR',
  recentPayments: [ { id: 'pay-81100', amountMinor: 3817 },
                    { id: 'pay-81150', amountMinor: 725 },
                    { id: 'pay-81200', amountMinor: 7134 } ] }

{ plan: 'SORT > COLLSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 0, docsExamined: 1000 }
{ plan: 'LIMIT > FETCH > IXSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 5, docsExamined: 5 }
{ plan: 'FETCH > SORT > IXSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 200, docsExamined: 5 }

Five payments went in and the array kept the last three. Read each plan from right to left: COLLSCAN is a collection scan (every document), IXSCAN walks the index, FETCH loads the documents the index points at, and SORT sorts in memory. Without the index MongoDB reads all 1,000 documents and sorts them. With it, it reads exactly 5 index entries and 5 documents. Drop status from the query and it walks all 200 index keys for M-0042, then sorts in memory: the index order is status first, so time order isn't free any more.

refs.title: MongoDB: the ESR (equality, sort, range) guideline

analogy: Think of a warehouse that ships orders. You can arrange the shelves by product, by customer or by delivery route, but each building has only one arrangement. If the shelves are arranged by customer, picking one customer's whole order is a short walk; finding every box of one product means walking the whole building. Rent a second building arranged by route and you can load route 7's truck in one walk, but every box now exists twice and every delivery to the warehouse has to stock both. Access-pattern modeling decides how many buildings you rent and how each one is arranged. The analogy breaks on upkeep: DynamoDB and MongoDB keep their indexes in step with the table for you, while two Cassandra tables are two buildings your own code has to stock.
world: Before your team moves the payment read model off Oracle, export a week of query statistics from your APM or from Oracle's AWR and list every statement against the payments tables with its rate and p99. That list is your access-pattern list, already measured. The authorization path will show payment-by-id and idempotency-key checks at thousands per second; the merchant dashboard shows the status-and-time query a few times per second; the finance export is a full read once a night and should stay one, fed from a Kafka topic into a copy built for it. A Temporal workflow that looks a payment up by id on every activity retry is AP2 again, which is one more reason to make it a key lookup.
mistake: The most common mistake is designing the tables first and the queries later, then reaching for a filter when a query doesn't fit. In DynamoDB that's a Scan or a Query with a FilterExpression; in Cassandra it's ALLOW FILTERING; in MongoDB it's a query with no index that matches. It works in development with 500 rows and falls over in production with 50 million, because the cost tracks the table, not the answer. People do it because the relational habit says "model the entities and the optimizer handles the rest". The fix: list the access patterns with their rates first, and treat any filter on a hot path as a missing key or index.

compare.title: AP1 in Oracle and in Cassandra

a.label: Oracle: normalize, join at read
a.title: Oracle: normalize, join at read
a.html: -- one table per entity; any query can come later CREATE TABLE payment ( payment_id VARCHAR2(20) PRIMARY KEY, account_id VARCHAR2(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES account, merchant_id VARCHAR2(20) NOT NULL REFERENCES merchant, amount_minor NUMBER(19) NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL ); CREATE INDEX payment_acct_time ON payment (account_id, created_at DESC); SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount_minor, m.name FROM payment p JOIN merchant m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id WHERE p.account_id = 'A-1001' ORDER BY p.created_at DESC FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY;

b.label: Cassandra: one table per query
b.title: Cassandra: one table per query
b.html: -- the query decides the table; merchant_name is copied in when the payment is written CREATE TABLE payments_by_account ( account_id text, created_at timestamp, payment_id text, merchant_name text, amount_minor bigint, PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, payment_id ASC); SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, merchant_name FROM payments_by_account WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' LIMIT 20;

compare.note: Both return the same 20 payments. Oracle reads them through an index and joins the merchant's name at read time, so a merchant rename shows up everywhere at once, and tomorrow's new query just needs a new index or none. Cassandra copies the merchant's name into every payment row when it writes, so the read is one partition slice with no join. A rename then means rewriting old rows or living with the old name, and a new question means a new table.

worked.title: Design keys for the refunds service

steps.say: The refunds service has three questions. Write them as data, the way the lab does. R3 serves an approvals screen that lists a merchant's pending refunds, oldest first.
steps.code: val patterns = listOf( AccessPattern("R1 refunds of a payment, newest first", equals = setOf("paymentId"), orderBy = "createdAt"), AccessPattern("R2 refund by id", equals = setOf("refundId")), AccessPattern("R3 merchant's refunds awaiting approval, oldest first", equals = setOf("merchantId", "status"), orderBy = "createdAt"), )

steps.say: First draft: key the table by refundId, then add one index per other question. The merchant index sorts by time first, because time felt like the main thing.
steps.code: val draft = listOf( KeyIndex("table", partitionKey = listOf("refundId")), KeyIndex("byPayment", partitionKey = listOf("paymentId"), sortKey = listOf("createdAt")), KeyIndex("byMerchant", partitionKey = listOf("merchantId"), sortKey = listOf("createdAt", "status")), ) AccessPatternChecker.checkAll(patterns, draft).forEach(::println)

steps.say: R3 comes back as a scan. status = PENDING is an equality, but status is the second sort attribute, after createdAt. Pending refunds are spread across the whole time range, so the store would read the merchant's entire partition and filter it.
steps.code:
Verdict(pattern=R1 refunds of a payment, newest first, kind=RANGE_READ, index=byPayment)
Verdict(pattern=R2 refund by id, kind=KEY_LOOKUP, index=table)
Verdict(pattern=R3 merchant's refunds awaiting approval, oldest first, kind=SCAN, index=null)

steps.say: Put the equality before the order: (merchantId; status, createdAt). status = PENDING now fixes a leading part of the sort key, and the oldest-first order is the very next attribute. Every refund is now written three times, once per copy, and each copy answers a question on the list.
steps.code: KeyIndex("byMerchant", partitionKey = listOf("merchantId"), sortKey = listOf("status", "createdAt")) // Verdict(pattern=R3 merchant's refunds awaiting approval, oldest first, kind=RANGE_READ, index=byMerchant)

lab.title: Build an access-pattern checker, then fix the payments key design
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All nine fail. No Docker needed.
Write AccessPatternChecker.classify, following rules 1 to 5 in its KDoc. check and checkAll are given and call it. When you're done, eight tests pass and only the design test fails.

Open PaymentsKeyDesign.kt. The table is keyed by paymentId only, so AP2 is the only pattern it answers. Add indexes until AP1 and AP3 are range reads and AP2 and AP4 are key lookups. The test also checks that every index you add is the answer to at least one pattern.
Experiment: swap the order of the sort key in your merchant index and run the tests again. Watch AP3 turn into a scan, then put it back.
hints: Rule 1 is one line: if (!pattern.equals.containsAll(index.partitionKey)) return ReadKind.SCAN.

For rule 2, count with a while loop how many leading sort key attributes are in pattern.equals. Call that number fixed. Then index.sortKey.getOrNull(fixed) is the only attribute a range or an order may use.
For rule 3, build the list of usable attributes, index.partitionKey + index.sortKey.take(fixed), and check that it contains every attribute in pattern.equals.
For the design, go pattern by pattern. Whatever a pattern fixes with = goes into the partition key; for AP3, the status also goes first in the sort key, before the time.

drill.title: AP3 in CQL from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the CQL table that answers AP3 (a merchant's payments with one status in a time window) with one partition per merchant per day. Then write the SELECT for merchant M-0042's FAILED payments on 2026-11-07 after 09:00 UTC. Check the order of your clustering columns against the answer.

answer.html: CREATE TABLE payments_by_merchant_day ( merchant_id text, day date, status text, created_at timestamp, payment_id text, account_id text, amount_minor bigint, -- (partition key), then clustering columns: equality first, then the range PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id, day), status, created_at, payment_id) ); SELECT status, created_at, payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments_by_merchant_day WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND day = '2026-11-07' AND status = 'FAILED' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000';

recap: In DynamoDB and Cassandra you design from the queries: list every access pattern with its rate before you choose a key.
The partition key needs = on all its parts. The sort key gives cheap slices: = on a leading part, then one range on the next part, no gaps.
Every query is a key lookup, a range read or a scan. A filter on a non-key attribute still pays for everything it reads.
A pattern the key can't answer gets another copy of the data: a global secondary index, another Cassandra table, another MongoDB index. Each copy costs a write on every insert.
In MongoDB, embed what is read together and bounded, reference what grows without limit, and order compound index fields equality, sort, range.

explain.prompt: A teammate proposes a DynamoDB payments table keyed only by paymentId and says: "We'll handle the other queries with filters later." Explain what happens to AP1 and AP3 at 50 million payments, and what you would do instead.
explain.answer: With only paymentId in the key, the table can answer one question cheaply: a payment by its id. AP1 (an account's newest payments) and AP3 (a merchant's payments by status and time) don't name the partition key, so DynamoDB can't run them as a Query. They become Scans with a FilterExpression, and a filter runs after the read, so each request reads all 50 million items, page by page, to return twenty. That's slow, and it eats read capacity that the authorization path needs. Instead I'd write the access patterns down first and give each one a key: a global secondary index keyed by account with the creation time as the sort key for AP1, and one keyed by merchant with status, then time, in the sort key for AP3. Each write then updates three copies, but every read costs what it returns.

deeper.html:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition, chapter 7) splits secondary indexes in distributed stores into two kinds, and the split explains the designs in this lesson. The Partitioning track's lesson on secondary indexes across shards builds both.

A local index (Kleppmann says document-partitioned) lives with each partition and indexes only that partition's data. Writes stay cheap, because a write touches one partition and its own index. Reads by the indexed attribute must ask every partition and merge the answers, a scatter-gather. DynamoDB's local secondary indexes are local in this sense, and they share the table's partition key, so they only help queries that already know the partition. Cassandra's storage-attached indexes (SAI, new in 5.0) are local too.

A global index (term-partitioned) is partitioned by the indexed value itself, so a read by that value goes to one place. The cost moves to writes: one payment write may have to update index partitions on other machines. DynamoDB's global secondary indexes work this way and are updated asynchronously, so a read from a GSI can briefly miss a write the table already has. That's why GSIs offer only eventually consistent reads.

Cassandra's "one table per query" is a global index you maintain by hand: you choose the partitioning of each copy and your code writes both. Its materialized views tried to automate that and are still marked experimental, so most teams write the tables themselves.

In lesson 4, single-table design packs several of these patterns into one DynamoDB table by giving different item types different key prefixes. Read DeBrie's post before then. He's in favour of it, and he lists the cases where he wouldn't use it.
